title: Paris 2024: The Olympics That Reminded the World Why It Still Matters
summary: The Paris Olympics delivered moments that will be remembered for generations — from track and field drama to the opening ceremony on the Seine. We look back at what made the Games so extraordinary and what they meant for sport.
content:
Every Olympic Games carries the burden of expectation. Critics find fault. Logistics fail in some corner of the host city. Athletes who were supposed to win do not. And yet, every four years, the Olympics produces moments that silence the critics — moments that remind a watching world why sport, at its best, is unlike anything else human beings have created.

Paris 2024 delivered those moments in abundance. From an opening ceremony that turned the Seine into a stage, to track and field drama that had global audiences awake in the middle of the night, to the emergence of new champions who will carry the sport into the next decade, the Games exceeded almost every expectation placed on them.

The Opening Ceremony

The decision to hold the opening ceremony along the River Seine — the first time in Olympic history that the ceremony took place outside a stadium — was either inspired or catastrophic, depending on who you asked in the months before the Games. It turned out to be inspired beyond any reasonable expectation. Athletes paraded on boats along the river, past monuments that have defined Paris for centuries, while performances unfolded along the banks and bridges. It was a celebration of French culture and an expression of civic pride that set the tone for everything that followed.

Track and Field: The Events That Defined the Games

The 100m final. The 1500m. The sprint hurdles. Athletics at the Paris Games produced a series of events that will be discussed for years. Noah Lyles, the American sprinter who had promised to deliver a performance for the ages, made good on that promise in the most dramatic possible way — winning the 100m by the smallest margin modern photo-finish technology could measure.

The women's events were equally compelling. Faith Kipyegon, the Kenyan middle-distance runner who is widely regarded as the greatest female 1500m runner in history, delivered a performance in the final that left observers searching for words adequate to describe what they had witnessed.

When you stand on that start line at the Olympics, everything you have done — every early morning, every painful session, every sacrifice — either prepared you for this moment or it didn't. There is nowhere to hide. And that is what makes it the greatest stage in sport.

The Swimming Pool

La Défense Arena produced some of the most dramatic swimming of the Olympic era. World records fell in events that observers thought had reached the limits of human performance. The relay events — always among the most emotionally charged in the Games — delivered finishes that had team benches erupting and commentators losing their composure.

The Host City

Paris itself was perhaps the greatest achievement of the Games. A city that many feared would struggle with security, transport, and the sheer logistics of hosting hundreds of thousands of visitors delivered an experience that reminded everyone why the choice of host city matters. The venues — many of them iconic Parisian landmarks adapted for sport — gave the Games a visual identity unlike any previous Olympics. Beach volleyball in the shadow of the Eiffel Tower. Equestrian events at Versailles. Fencing in the Grand Palais.

What They Meant

Every Olympics matters because it represents something beyond sport: the idea that competition between nations can be conducted with mutual respect, that the best athletes in the world can be in the same place at the same time, that the pursuit of excellence is a universal value. Paris delivered on all of it.

The 2028 Games go to Los Angeles. They have a very high bar to clear.
